## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.
I’ll read the last two reviews, retain 20k, and play game 126 to completion. I’ll check whole-group life and early area, then save the game and lessons for the next session.

const review=`# Game 126: White vs 20k — W+14

Played 2026-10-06. 9×9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
White80/Black81 passes ended the game; board() confirmed W+14, next move82.
Independent displayed area White44/Black37, neutral0; no dead removal needed.
Physical captures Black0/White15. Every final White stone survived in two groups:
left25 stones/29 area with true A4/B6/C1/C5;
right13 stones/15 area with true H9/J6.
Completed20k record:22 wins/94 losses/5 draws; game87 unfinished and excluded. Retain20k.

## Evidence and limits

Read125/124 and consulted122 before selecting20k on a confirmed empty White board.
Preserved initial board, selection with Black1 E5, all40 play responses and final confirmation:43 raw snapshots.
Actual-history replay legally reproduced all81 moves and matched every board, physical capture count, next move number and ko marker.
Live full programmatic inspections were after27/55/69; final full inspection was after81.
After-own-move details in verification are retrospective replay, not additional live observations.
No invalid submission, ko, resignation, missing response or transport failure.
All move choices and hypothetical reading were manual. Code only inspected current boards, counted groups/area, kept records, replayed actual history and converted it to SGF.
No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search, automated move selection/ranking/recommendation or delegation.

This win depended on weak actual defenses. Black27 F9 allowed G9 to atari H9; Black29 F8 ignored that atari.
Black49 E3 ignored D4's atari, allowing a capture that reopened a real connection.
The eventual left six-stone chain had only one enemy-bordered two-point space and no escape.
No optimal opening, earlier winning substitution or individual move value is established.
Game52's unresolved score and game99/106's raw-evidence limits remain separate.

## Exact moves

${movesText}

## Early width and an open right base

C3/C7 took the left corners against Black E5/F3/F7.
D3 at6 joined C3 and widened the lower boundary.
D2 at8 joined D3 and retained the inward bottom endpoint after Black E2.
Black D7 contacted C7; extending the left alone risked a narrow side without enough area.
G5 at10 took the still-open right side before later caps.
This was an early second base, not a late replacement invasion.
G6/G4 at12/14 joined G5. Black G7 and H4 capped the upper and lower sides.
H5 at16 joined G5; Black J4 joined H4 and closed the lower edge.

The first exact reference used during live manual reading after19 looked back to the after11 position:
ABC all rows =27;
D1/D2/D3 =3;
GHJ rows4–6 =9;
HJ rows7–9 =6;
total45.
By the time that ledger was formed, Black H4/J4 had already taken two reference points, so the remaining proposed reference was43.
This was conditional, unsealed and without eye proof, not secure current area.
The exact ledger was not recorded at move11 itself.
The right reference deliberately excluded G7/G8/G9 beside Black F7; eventual G8/G9 were outside gains.

## Right containment, endpoint work and two separate eyes

H7 at18 began SEPARATE from the G4/G5/G6/H5 main.
H8 at20 joined H7 and kept the upper escape/eye boundary open.
Black21 J6 entered between the two White chains.
J5 at22 joined H5 and blocked J6 from joining Black J4.
Black23 J7 extended J6; J8 at24 joined H8 and left the invaders sole H6.
Black H6 would join J6/J7 but leave no liberty and capture neither White chain, which retained other liberties. It was suicide at this point.

Black25 H9 entered the top endpoint with G9/J9 liberties.
G8 at26 joined H8 and retained access to G9.
Black27 F9 capped the left but did not occupy G9.
G9 at28 joined G8 and ataried H9 at J9.
Black29 F8 connected F9 to F7/G7 but left H9 in atari.
J9 at30 captured H9 while joining J8; the capture reopened H9.
H9 became a true one-point eye bounded by G9/H8/J9.

Black31 F6 joined its central and upper chains.
H6 at32 captured J6/J7 and ACTUALLY joined the lower and upper White chains.
The reopened J6/J7 two-point room was independent of H9, supplying the second eye.
This capture added a connection and restored reference points; it did not create new territory outside the ledger.
There was no ko.

Black71 J6 later re-entered with sole J7.
White72 J7 captured it and joined H7/J8, leaving true J6.
Final right13+2=15; H9/J6 remained independent throughout the closing passes.

## Left bases and the bottom invasion

Black33 C5 entered the left side.
C6 at34 joined C7; Black B6 began separate.
B7 at36 joined C7 and blocked B6 upward access.
Black B4 entered below the prospective divider.
B3 at38 joined C3 and blocked its lower route.
Black39 A3 began separate at A2/A4.
A2 at40 began separate with A1/B2, but had an actual immediate join available at B2.
After Black41 A4 joined A3 to B4, B2 at42 ACTUALLY joined A2 to B3/main.
This differs from game124's failed D2/B6 cuts: the next extension reached the friendly chain.

Black43 C1 invaded with B1/C2/D1 liberties.
D1 at44 joined D2 and removed the escape toward E1.
Black45 B1 joined C1, leaving A1/C2.
The lower White group still had no completed two-eye proof.
An immediate two-step capture through A1/C2 would consume both boundary points and leave only one connected B1/C1 room.
I therefore continued to look for real connection/room before clearing these invaders.
The later rescue depended on Black's D4 mistake; the earlier lower play is not proved sound against stronger replies.

## D4 capture reopened a junction

C4 at46 joined C3 and capped C5 below.
Black47 D4 began separate with D5/E4, adjacent to White C4/D3.
E4 at48 began separate with E3/F4 and ataried D4 at D5.
Black49 E3 joined BOTH E2 and F3, capped E4 at F4, and ignored the D4 atari.

A live mental error briefly treated E3 as suicide after E4 because of the surrounding stones.
That was wrong: adjacent BLACK E2/F3 were friendly to Black E3 and supplied inherited liberties.
The actual E3 response corrected the reading. No invalid move was submitted.
Always identify the mover's friendly neighboring chains before assessing suicide.

D5 at50 captured D4.
The new D5 stone had D4/D6 liberties and did not yet join either White chain.
Crucially, removing D4 also reopened D4 for E4 and the lower C4/D3 chain.
E4 now had D4 AND F4, so it was no longer the previously read one-liberty stone.
My manual reading initially considered sacrificing E4; the actual capture had changed that premise.

Black51 B5 joined B6/C5 and A3/A4/B4 into one six-stone chain.
D4 at52 then ACTUALLY joined D5, E4 and the lower main.
Black53 F4 connected its central and bottom chains, blocking the rightward connection.
D6 at54 ACTUALLY joined D5/main to C6/C7/B7.
The lower and upper White bases were now one group.
This was a capture-reopened junction followed by real orthogonal joins, not a diagonal rescue.

## Connected approach to the confined left chain

After D6, Black A3/A4/B4/B5/B6/C5 had only A5/A6.
Those two points were one enemy-bordered room, not two eyes.
Playing White A5 immediately would be self-atari at A6 and allow Black A6 to capture the attacker, reopening A5. I withheld it.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
